Neither Ethiopian nor English, neither lucky nor crazy, a capacious bird humming as he penned in his mind another enflamed letter to President Jefferson—he imagined the reply, polite and rhetorical. At dawn he milked the cows, then went inside and put on a pot to stew while he slept. The clock he whittled as a boy still ran. Neighbors woke him up with warm bread and quilts. Lowering his eyes to fields sweet with the rot of spring, he could see a government’s domed city rising from the morass and spreading in a spiral of lights....

At nightfall he took out his rifle—a white-maned figure stalking the darkened breast of the Union—and fired at the stars, and by chance one went out. Had he killed?

I assure thee, my dear Sir! Lowering his eyes to fields sweet with the rot of spring, he could see a government’s domed city rising from the morass and spreading in a spiral of lights....
outputs.L2:
What was he ever doing, other than lying beneath a pear tree, bundled in an enormous cloak, contemplating the celestial bodies?

“Venerable,” the decent citizens of Baltimore murmured—startled, uneasy, and somewhat frightened. It was rumored, of course, that he had become fond of hard liquor. What other explanation could there be for his spending whole nights outdoors beneath the stars? And why had he never taken a wife? Then again, who would have him? He was neither Ethiopian nor English, neither blessed nor mad—like some large, humming bird, silently composing in his head yet another fiery letter to President Jefferson, while picturing the answer he would receive: courteous, polished, and full of grand phrases. Travelers who had visited Philadelphia said that the statue of Benjamin Franklin standing before the library matched him in size and appearance.

A wife? Certainly not.

At daybreak he milked the cows; afterward he went indoors, set a pot to simmer, and slept. The clock he had carved with his own hands as a boy was still working. His neighbors roused him with fresh warm bread and blankets. When evening came, he brought out his rifle—a white-haired figure moving across the shadowed heart of the Union—and fired at the stars. By accident, one of them disappeared.

Had he struck it down?

I assure thee, my dear Sir! As he dropped his gaze toward fields fragrant with springtime decay, he could envision the domed city of a government rising out of the swamp, widening outward in a spiral of lights....
outputs.L3:
Each night, the man makes his way to the shelter of a pear tree, where he studies the stars and lets his imagination travel far beyond the limits of his daily life. Beneath its branches, he composes letters in his mind to President Jefferson, addressing the leader of the young nation as though they were engaged in an intimate and serious exchange. These imagined letters reveal both his intellectual ambition and his desire to be heard by a country that does not fully recognize him.

The people of Baltimore regard him with suspicion and unease. They gossip about his solitary habits, his drinking, and the fact that he has never married. To them, his independence and privacy seem strange, even threatening. Rather than understanding his brilliance, they reduce him to rumor and speculation, measuring him against the social expectations he refuses or fails to meet.

He is presented as an outsider, someone who belongs completely to neither Black nor white society. This in-between position isolates him, but it also gives him a distinctive perspective. Though others may dismiss or misunderstand him, he possesses an extraordinary intellect and a powerful imagination. His mind moves between mathematics, astronomy, invention, and political vision, making him far more complex than the judgments of his neighbors suggest.

His daily life combines ordinary physical labor with remarkable acts of thought and creativity. He milks cows, prepares food, and attends to the practical demands of survival, yet these simple routines exist alongside moments of invention, calculation, and deep contemplation. The contrast emphasizes the breadth of his life: he is both a laboring man rooted in the material world and a visionary capable of imagining vast structures, celestial patterns, and national futures.

The passage connects his stargazing to the larger story of the emerging United States. As he watches the heavens, his visions expand toward the shape of the nation itself, including the imagined rise of a domed government city. His private observations beneath the pear tree become linked to public history, architecture, and power. In this way, the passage presents him not merely as a solitary dreamer, but as a figure whose imagination reaches toward the possibilities and contradictions of a new republic.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents an eccentric and solitary Black astronomer living on the outskirts of Baltimore, a man whose life appears ordinary from a distance but becomes extraordinary when viewed closely. By day, he is connected to the world of practical labor, rural routines, and neighborhood gossip. People know him through fragments: his habits, his strangeness, his race, his intelligence, and the rumors that gather around anyone who lives too much apart from others. He belongs to a humble world of fields, tools, weather, and work, yet his mind is constantly drawn upward, beyond the limits of his immediate surroundings.

At night, his isolation becomes a form of freedom. While others sleep, he studies the heavens, watching the movement of stars and planets with patience and precision. The sky gives him a language larger than the one available to him in ordinary society. Through astronomy, he enters into a vast order that ignores earthly hierarchies, including the racial and social barriers that define the young United States. His observations are not merely scientific; they are also imaginative and spiritual. The stars allow him to think about time, destiny, creation, and the place of human beings in the universe.

His imagined letters to Thomas Jefferson deepen this meaning. Jefferson represents the nation’s ideals of reason, liberty, and enlightenment, but he also represents its contradictions, especially the coexistence of freedom and slavery. By writing to Jefferson, or imagining himself in conversation with him, the astronomer places himself inside the intellectual and moral debates of the republic. He claims a voice in a nation that might otherwise ignore him. His letters become acts of self-assertion, showing that wisdom and vision can arise from someone excluded from power.

The passage therefore makes the astronomer more than a curious local figure. He becomes a symbol of solitary brilliance: a person whose quiet life connects the most modest daily realities to the largest questions of science, politics, and morality. His existence challenges assumptions about race, knowledge, and authority. In him, the domestic and the cosmic meet; the laborer becomes a thinker, the outsider becomes a witness, and the isolated observer becomes part of the nation’s imaginative foundation.

Through this figure, the passage suggests that the creation of the United States was not only the work of famous statesmen and public leaders. It was also shaped, and morally questioned, by those who stood at its margins. The astronomer’s gaze toward the stars becomes a way of measuring the country itself: its ambitions, its failures, and its unfinished promise.

**What Makes Baltimore Venerable**

What gives a city its character is not only its buildings, streets, or landmarks, but the stories carried by the people who live there. Baltimore is a city with a venerable history, shaped by generations of workers, artists, immigrants, and leaders who helped define its identity.

Known for its historic harbor, distinctive neighborhoods, and cultural traditions, Baltimore has long played an important role in American history. From its connection to “The Star-Spangled Banner” to its legacy in industry, education, and the arts, the city stands as a place of resilience and reinvention.

The word **venerable** suggests something respected because of age, dignity, and lasting importance. In that sense, Baltimore is truly venerable. It honors its past while continuing to grow and adapt. Its old row houses, churches, markets, and museums remind visitors that history is still alive in the city’s daily life.

What makes Baltimore special is its combination of heritage and spirit. It is a city that has faced challenges but continues to inspire pride, creativity, and community. Baltimore’s venerable presence remains an essential part of its charm and strength.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical historical fiction passage about Benjamin Banneker in a style reminiscent of literary magical realism, focusing on his solitude, astronomy, correspondence with Jefferson, and the founding of Washington, D.C.
counterfactuals.output:
At night, when the fields of Maryland surrendered their heat and the tobacco leaves hung like dark green hands in prayer, Benjamin Banneker climbed into the sky by means of numbers.

He did not need a ladder. He had his almanacs, his worn instruments, his table spread with paper, ink, and the delicate bones of calculation. Above his cabin, the heavens turned with the solemn patience of a millwheel, and he, a free Black man alone among orchards and boundary stones, listened to their machinery. The stars spoke in fractions. The moon loosened her silver hair over the Patapsco. Time, which had once been taught to him by a borrowed watch and the secret pulse of wooden gears, came now like a familiar animal to his door.

The neighbors said old Banneker hardly slept. They saw his candle burning after midnight, a small earthly star answering the celestial multitude. They did not know that in those hours the room expanded until its rafters held constellations, until Saturn brushed the chimney soot from his rings, until comets dragged their luminous tails through the margins of his papers. He bent over eclipses as another man might bend over scripture, and in the arithmetic of shadow he found a God who did not segregate light.

Solitude was his companion, but not his jailer. It sat beside him while he calculated the courses of planets, while frost whitened the fields and summer insects rasped in the grass. It held the inkpot steady when, in 1791, he wrote to Thomas Jefferson—statesman, philosopher, slaveholder—with the courtesy of a gentleman and the force of a bell tolling across a valley. He enclosed an almanac, proof made not of argument alone but of the moon’s obedient return, the tides of heaven predicted by a man whose people had been called incapable of reason.

The letter traveled north and south through a country still soft from birth, carrying with it the scent of candle smoke and Maryland soil. In Philadelphia, in Virginia, in the chambers where liberty was spoken like a polished language, the pages rustled. Jefferson read them beneath the shadow of his own contradictions. For a moment, perhaps, the ink shimmered. Perhaps the planets Banneker had charted leaned over Jefferson’s shoulder and looked down sternly upon the words. Perhaps the future capital, not yet risen from swamp and surveyor’s dream, stirred in its sleep.

Banneker had walked that future ground.

He had stood among the men appointed to mark the Federal City, where the Potomac curved like a brown arm through marsh and forest. Surveying chains flashed in the sun; stakes were driven; lines were pulled across farms and creeks, over graves and wildflowers, through the haunts of heron and fox. Pierre L’Enfant imagined avenues broad enough for empire. Others measured angles, distances, claims. Banneker, with his astronomical clockwork in his mind, lifted his eyes from the mud to the meridian and found the city’s place beneath the stars.

The land was unruly then, full of mosquitoes and prophecy. At dawn the mist rose so thickly from the river that the surveyors seemed to walk inside an unmade map. Sometimes, it was said, the boundary stones hummed after Banneker passed, as if remembering the coordinates he had whispered. Sometimes the compass needle trembled, not from iron, but from the nearness of destiny. A capital was being summoned from reed beds and red clay, and every line drawn upon the earth was answered by an invisible line in the heavens.

Yet when the city began to exist—first as plan, then as rumor, then as cleared ground and stubborn ambition—it carried within it a silence shaped like him. No marble dome had yet risen; no grand avenue had yet filled with carriages, soldiers, petitioners, presidents. But Banneker had already placed the stars above it. He had given to the republic, which did not yet know how to give him justice, the precision of his mind.

In the evenings he returned to his farm, to the bees, the fruit trees, the patient dark. The world might reduce him to an exception, a curiosity, a footnote written in another man’s hand. But the sky made no such mistake. It opened for him nightly, immense and exact, and called him by his full name.

There, alone with the constellations, Benjamin Banneker continued his correspondence with eternity. His ink dried; his candle guttered; the owl spoke from the edge of the woods. Far away, Jefferson’s Monticello gleamed on its hill like a pale question. Farther still, the unborn city waited beside the Potomac, its avenues folded like wings.

And above them all the heavens revolved—not indifferent, but remembering—while Banneker counted, wrote, and listened, a solitary man holding a republic to the measure of the stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, poetic paragraph imagining an elderly Black astronomer in early America lying beneath a pear tree, viewed suspiciously by his Baltimore neighbors, blending biography, myth, and surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output: Beneath the pear tree in Baltimore County, where the fruit hung like small green planets in a private firmament, the old Black astronomer lay with his coat folded under his head and the whole suspicious neighborhood peering from shutters, lanes, and scripture-darkened doorways, wondering whether he slept, calculated, conjured, or conversed with powers better left unnamed. They had watched him all his life—watched the free dark son of a freedwoman and an African man carve time into wooden gears, coax eclipses from ink, send almanacs into the young republic like black stars through a white sky, and write to Jefferson as if liberty were not a locked orchard. Now, under the tree, his face was a weathered moon, his hands root-knotted and still, while above him pears ripened into comets, bees orbited like golden satellites, and the heavens lowered their blue, crowded brow to listen. Some said he was only Banneker, old Ben, harmless and peculiar; others saw a sorcerer measuring God’s pulse with a pocket watch, a man who had stolen the night’s arithmetic and hidden it in his bones. But the tree knew him otherwise: as a boy of clay and starlight, as a surveyor of invisible kingdoms, as a myth walking in homespun, who mapped the capital of a nation that could not map his freedom, and who now rested between earth and cosmos while the neighbors, afraid of his silence, mistook the universe bending down for a shadow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a novelistic vignette about Benjamin Banneker that mentions his wooden clock, his letters to Thomas Jefferson, rumors about his drinking and bachelorhood, and a dreamlike vision of the capital city rising from a swamp.
counterfactuals.output:
At night, when the frogs stitched the marsh-dark with their throats and the Maryland air lay wet against the windowpanes, Benjamin Banneker listened to the clock.

It was not a grand clock, not brass-faced and imported from London, but a thing he had coaxed out of wood with his own patient hands: wheels, teeth, pins, a small universe of motion hidden in a case. Years ago he had taken apart a borrowed watch, studied its secret ministry, and returned from that bright captivity with a design that ticked beside him now as if it possessed a heart. The neighbors said it was a wonder. Banneker, who had learned that wonders could be made by rule and measure, heard in it not magic but proof.

Tick: a star found its place.

Tick: a number answered another.

Tick: the night diminished.

On the table lay his papers—astronomical calculations, inked columns, almanac drafts, letters folded and unfolded until the creases softened like cloth. One of those letters had gone to Thomas Jefferson, the famous Virginian, author of liberty in a country still wearing chains. Banneker had written with courtesy, with Scripture, with the contained fire of a man who had measured the heavens and would not be measured small by other men. He had sent his almanac as evidence: not a plea, exactly, but a demonstration. Here, sir. Observe.

Jefferson had replied politely, too politely perhaps, praising the effort, passing the proof onward as if genius were a specimen to be labeled and displayed. Still, Banneker kept the exchange. A letter could be a tool. A letter could be a lever set beneath the weight of an age.

Beyond the door his farm slept in uneven patches of moonlight. He was a free Black man in a land that could not decide what freedom meant. He was a surveyor, a calculator of eclipses, a maker of tables by candle and quill. He was also, in the loose court of neighborhood tongues, a bachelor too long alone, a man too fond—some whispered—of the bottle. Rumor came and went like weather. It leaned over fences, paused in taverns, entered churches under bonnets and hats. Banneker knew of it. He knew the pity some attached to bachelorhood, as if solitude were an illness, and the relish with which others embroidered a man’s habits into a garment meant to fit him forever.

Let them talk, he thought sometimes.

Yet even rumors had weight at night. They hovered in corners with the smoke.

He rose, opened the door, and stepped into the damp. The sky above Ellicott’s Mills was immense, the stars fixed and declarative. Somewhere beyond the sleeping fields lay the place he had helped survey—the chosen ground for the nation’s capital, low and muddy along the Potomac, rank with reeds, insects, and the breath of standing water. Men with chains and compasses had gone over it, marking lines where streets would be, where avenues would cut broad diagonals through the wilderness, where power imagined itself in stone.

He closed his eyes and saw it.

Not as it was, a swamp murmuring under the moon, but as a dream rising from vapor: domes pale as planets, columns lifting through mist, avenues unspooling like geometric promises. He saw carts sinking to their axles, enslaved men hauling timber, survey stakes glowing like little flames. He saw a city not yet born already burdened with contradiction. White walls climbed out of black mud. Marble shone with the labor it tried to forget. At the center of it all, a great silence opened, waiting for speeches, parades, petitions, laws.

In the dream, the capital rose and sank at once.

Banneker stood at its edge with his instruments in hand, feeling the pull of numbers against the unruliness of earth. A city could be plotted. So could an eclipse. But justice—what instrument, what quadrant, what table could predict its arrival? He had seen planets return faithfully to their appointed places. Men were less obedient to heaven.

The clock inside the house struck the hour, its wooden voice carrying through the damp like a small, stubborn proclamation.

He opened his eyes. The swamp-city vanished. There was only his field, the smell of grass, the night insects clicking in the brush. But the vision remained lodged in him: a capital lifted from marsh and contradiction, a republic drawing lines across the land while failing to read the plainest line in its own founding words.

Banneker went back inside. The candle had guttered low, bending over his papers. He sat, trimmed the wick, and took up his pen.

The clock ticked on, wooden and exact. Outside, rumors moved in the dark. Above, the stars kept their luminous order. And Benjamin Banneker, unmarried, watched, doubted, calculated, endured—setting down numbers against oblivion, setting down words against silence, as if both might yet strike the hour.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose excerpt in the voice of a contemporary literary author, portraying Benjamin Banneker as a strange, revered figure who studies the stars, lives alone, and becomes half legend among his neighbors.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in the exact voice of a specific contemporary author, but here’s an original experimental prose excerpt with a contemporary literary sensibility:

---

By then the old man on the hill had become less a man than a weather.

Children were warned against the edge of his orchard, though no one could say what harm had ever come from it. Women passing with baskets lowered their voices. Men who had borrowed his calculations, his seed, his clockwork sense of seasons, spoke of him afterward as if they had received a favor from the dark itself. Benjamin Banneker, they said, lived alone among ticks and gears, among bees and pages, among instruments whose names changed depending on who was frightened enough to describe them.

At night his cabin burned with a patient light.

Not a hearth-light. Not the common animal glow of supper, socks steaming, a kettle’s iron mutter. His was a thin flame, mathematical, as if he had trapped a star under glass and taught it to behave. Through the trees one could see him sometimes: a narrow figure bent over a table, then suddenly upright, as though answering to a voice above the roof.

He watched the heavens the way other men watched roads.

Roads brought debt, rumor, soldiers, cousins, weather from the west, a horse gone lame, a letter edged in black. The heavens brought order, though not comfort. He knew this distinction. The stars did not love him. The moon did not bless his loneliness. Yet they returned when they were meant to return, and in that returning was a stern mercy he could almost trust.

In the village they made a second Banneker out of talk.

This Banneker did not sleep. This Banneker ate roots and numbers. This Banneker had built a clock from memory after seeing one only once, and inside the clock he had hidden a sermon, a map, a small wooden heart. This Banneker could predict an eclipse, a frost, a birthmark, the hour a guilty man would begin confessing to himself. This Banneker was not old but ancient, not Black but blue-black like the space between constellations, not human exactly, but something God had drafted in the margin and forgotten to explain.

The real Banneker rose with aching joints.

He boiled water. He sharpened his quill. He listened to the small complaints of the house: timber easing, mouse-foot, wind-finger at the chink. His solitude was not pure. It had splinters, invoices, hunger, the stubborn stink of damp wool. Some mornings his hands trembled so badly the numerals came out wounded. Some nights the sky clouded over and gave him nothing.

Still, he waited.

Waiting was one of his instruments.

Above him the constellations wheeled in their cold harness. Below, the county slept and invented him. By dawn, a boy would swear he had seen the old man standing in the field with both arms lifted, holding the moon in place. A farmer would claim his cattle calved early because Banneker had looked too long at Orion. Someone’s aunt would whisper that no person ought to know so much about what was coming.

And Banneker, hearing none of it or hearing all of it, dipped his pen again.

The page received him without fear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short piece of historical magical realism set in Maryland around 1800, featuring a mixed-race or Black mathematician-astronomer, Benjamin Franklin’s statue, President Jefferson, and a surreal moment where shooting at the stars makes one go out.
counterfactuals.output:
In the year 1800, when Maryland still smelled of tobacco leaf, wet clay, and the old arguments of liberty, Benjamin Banneker kept his clock wound against the dark.

He lived near Ellicott’s Mills, a free Black man with a surveyor’s chain, an astronomer’s eye, and figures moving through his mind like bright fish beneath ice. At night he stood outside his cabin and measured the heavens, writing columns of numbers by lantern-light while the woods whispered in English, French, and languages older than both.

One autumn evening, President Thomas Jefferson passed through Baltimore on business of the young republic. In a public square there stood a statue of Benjamin Franklin—bronze-faced, kite-string in hand, spectacles catching moonlight though no moon had risen. Jefferson paused before it, considering the dead philosopher as if awaiting advice.

Banneker, summoned by curiosity or by some arithmetic of fate, approached with his almanac tucked beneath his arm.

“Mr. Banneker,” Jefferson said, recognizing the name from the letter that had once chastened him more precisely than any sermon, “do your stars still keep time?”

“They do,” Banneker replied, “though men often do not.”

At that moment a militia boy nearby, drunk on cider and independence, raised his musket toward the sky. “Let’s see if Heaven bleeds!” he shouted, and fired.

The crack rolled over the rooftops. Sparks leapt from the muzzle. High above, one star—small, blue-white, and ancient—shuddered like a candle in a draft.

Then it went out.

Silence fell. Even the horses stopped breathing. Franklin’s bronze head turned with a soft grinding sound, and his metal eyes fixed on Jefferson.

Banneker opened his almanac, found the missing star’s place, and drew a careful black circle around the absence.

Jefferson whispered, “Can it be restored?”

Banneker looked from the president to the statue to the wounded sky.

“Perhaps,” he said. “But first the republic must learn the difference between aiming upward and understanding what it sees.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
